### A.1 Anomalous dimension of the operator $S_{a}=c^{{\dagger}}_{\textbf{a}_{1}}T^{a}_{\textbf{a}_{1}\textbf{a}_{2}}c_{\textbf{a}_{2}}$

We would like to compute anomalous dimension of the operator $S_{a}(\tau)=c^{{\dagger}}_{\textbf{a}_{1}}(\tau)T^{a}_{\textbf{a}_{1}\textbf{a}_{2}}c_{\textbf{a}_{2}}(\tau)$ . First of all we notice that it has bare dimension $[S_{a}]=[\mu]^{1-r}$ . On the other hand the operator $\phi_{a}(\tau,x=0)$ has bare dimension $[\phi_{a}]=[\mu]^{\frac{d-1}{2}}$ , therefore when $r\to 1/2$ and $d\to 2$ these two operators can mix. Thus we define renormalized dimensionless operators as

$$ \displaystyle[S_{a}(\tau)]_{R}=Z_{SS}\mu^{r-1}S_{a}(\tau)+Z_{S\phi}\mu^{\frac{1-d}{2}}\phi_{a}(\tau,0)\,, \displaystyle[\phi_{a}(\tau)]_{R}=Z_{\phi S}\mu^{r-1}S_{a}(\tau)+Z_{\phi\phi}\mu^{\frac{1-d}{2}}\phi_{a}(\tau,0)\,, $$

where the counter-terms have only poles in $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon^{\prime}$ and have the following form

$$ \displaystyle Z_{SS}=1+z_{SS}^{(1)}(U,V,\gamma,\zeta,\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime})+z_{SS}^{(2)}(U,V,\gamma,\zeta,\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime})+\dots\,, \displaystyle Z_{S\phi}=z_{S\phi}^{(1)}(U,V,\gamma,\zeta,\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime})+z_{S\phi}^{(2)}(U,V,\gamma,\zeta,\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime})+\dots\,, \displaystyle Z_{\phi S}=z_{\phi S}^{(1)}(U,V,\gamma,\zeta,\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime})+z_{\phi S}^{(2)}(U,V,\gamma,\zeta,\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime})+\dots\,, \displaystyle Z_{\phi\phi}=1+z_{\phi\phi}^{(1)}(U,V,\gamma,\zeta,\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime})+z_{\phi\phi}^{(2)}(U,V,\gamma,\zeta,\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime})+\dots\,, $$

and as usual $\epsilon=1-2r$ and $\epsilon^{\prime}=2-d$ . It is convenient to work in momentum space so we have

$$ \displaystyle[S_{a}(\omega)]_{R}=Z_{SS}\mu^{r-1}S_{a}(\omega)+Z_{S\phi}\mu^{\frac{1-d}{2}}\int\frac{d^{d}k}{(2\pi)^{d}}\phi_{a}(\omega,k)\,. $$

We find the counter-terms $Z_{SS}$ , $Z_{S\phi}$ , $Z_{\phi S}$ and $Z_{\phi\phi}$ by demanding that expressions

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{SS}(\omega|\omega^{\prime})=\frac{\langle[S_{a}(\omega)]_{R}c_{\textbf{a}_{1}}(\omega^{\prime})c^{{\dagger}}_{\textbf{a}_{2}}(\omega+\omega^{\prime})\rangle_{c}}{G(\omega^{\prime})G(\omega+\omega^{\prime})},\quad\Gamma_{S\phi}(\omega|k)=\frac{\langle[S_{a}(\omega)]_{R}\phi_{b}(-\omega,-k)\rangle_{c}}{D(\omega,k)}\,, \displaystyle\Gamma_{\phi S}(\omega|\omega^{\prime})=\frac{\langle[\phi_{a}(\omega)]_{R}c_{\textbf{a}_{1}}(\omega^{\prime})c^{{\dagger}}_{\textbf{a}_{2}}(\omega+\omega^{\prime})\rangle_{c}}{G(\omega^{\prime})G(\omega+\omega^{\prime})},\quad\Gamma_{\phi\phi}(\omega|k)=\frac{\langle[\phi_{a}(\omega)]_{R}\phi_{b}(-\omega,-k)\rangle_{c}}{D(\omega,k)} $$

are free of divergencies, where $G(\omega)=\langle c(\omega)c^{{\dagger}}(\omega)\rangle$ and $D(\omega,k)=\langle\phi(\omega,k)\phi(-\omega,-k)\rangle=1/(\omega^{2}+k^{2})$ . To the leading order we can write expressions for (64) as

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{SS}(\omega|\omega^{\prime})=Z_{SS}\mu^{r-1}(1+A)+Z_{S\phi}\mu^{\frac{1-d}{2}}B\,, \displaystyle\Gamma_{S\phi}(\omega|k)=Z_{SS}\mu^{r-1}C+Z_{S\phi}\mu^{\frac{1-d}{2}}(1+D)\,, \displaystyle\Gamma_{\phi S}(\omega|\omega^{\prime})=Z_{\phi S}\mu^{r-1}(1+A)+Z_{\phi\phi}\mu^{\frac{1-d}{2}}B\,, \displaystyle\Gamma_{\phi\phi}(\omega|k)=Z_{\phi S}\mu^{r-1}C+Z_{\phi\phi}\mu^{\frac{1-d}{2}}(1+D)\,, $$

where diagrams $A,B,C$ and $D$ are listed in figure 12.

*Figure 12: All leading order diagrams for renormalization of operators $S_{a}$ and $\phi_{a}$ .*

Computing the diagrams we find the counter-terms

$$ \displaystyle z_{ss}^{(1)}=\frac{U+M^{\prime}V}{\pi A_{0}^{2}}\frac{1}{\epsilon},\quad z_{s\phi}^{(1)}=-\frac{M^{\prime}\gamma}{2\pi A_{0}^{2}}\frac{1}{\epsilon}\quad z_{\phi s}^{(1)}=\frac{\gamma}{2\pi}\frac{1}{\epsilon^{\prime}},\quad z_{\phi\phi}^{(1)}=\frac{\zeta}{2\pi}\frac{1}{\epsilon^{\prime}}\,. $$

Therefore the matrix of anomalous dimensions is

$$ \displaystyle\gamma_{ij}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-\frac{U+M^{\prime}V}{\pi A_{0}^{2}}&\frac{M^{\prime}\gamma}{2\pi A_{0}^{2}}\\
\frac{\gamma}{2\pi}&\frac{\zeta}{2\pi}\\
\end{array}\right)\,. $$

The full scaling dimensions are obtained by adding $\textrm{diag}(1-r,\frac{d-1}{2})$ to $\gamma_{ij}$ and diagonalizing the full matrix.

### A.2 Stability of fixed points

In this subsection we discuss the stability of fixed points found above and listed in Eqs. (39) - (42). First we construct the stability matrix,

$$ J\equiv\begin{bmatrix}J_{1}&J_{2}&J_{3}\\
J_{4}&J_{5}&J_{6}\\
J_{7}&J_{8}&J_{9}\end{bmatrix}\,, $$

where,

$$ \displaystyle J_{1} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{\partial\beta_{\gamma}}{\partial\gamma}=\frac{\epsilon-\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}-\frac{U}{\pi A_{0}^{2}}+\frac{\zeta}{2\pi}\,,~~~~J_{2}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta_{\gamma}}{\partial U}=-\frac{\gamma}{\pi A_{0}^{2}}\,,~~~~J_{3}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta_{\gamma}}{\partial\zeta}=\frac{\gamma}{2\pi}\,, \displaystyle J_{4} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{\partial\beta_{U}}{\partial\gamma}=-\frac{3\gamma}{4\pi}\,,~~~~J_{5}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta_{U}}{\partial U}=\epsilon\,,~~~~J_{6}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta_{U}}{\partial\zeta}=0\,, \displaystyle J_{7} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{\partial\beta_{\zeta}}{\partial\gamma}=\frac{\gamma}{\pi A_{0}^{2}}\,,~~~~J_{8}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta_{\zeta}}{\partial U}=0\,,~~~~J_{9}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta_{\zeta}}{\partial\zeta}=-\epsilon^{\prime}+\frac{\zeta}{\pi}\,. $$

The eigenvalues of matrix $J$ at the trivial fixed points (39) and (40) are $(\epsilon,(\epsilon-\epsilon^{\prime})/2,-\epsilon^{\prime})$ and $(\epsilon,(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})/2,\epsilon^{\prime})$ respectively. Thus, for any positive values of $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon^{\prime}$ all the eigenvalues corresponding to $FP_{2}$ are positive, and thus it is a stable fixed point. The eigenvalues at the non-trivial fixed points (41) and (42) are given by the roots of their respective characteristic polynomials,

$$ p_{3}(\lambda)=\lambda^{3}+a_{3}\lambda^{2}+b_{3}\lambda+c_{3}\,,~~~p_{4}(\lambda)=\lambda^{3}+a_{4}\lambda^{2}+b_{4}\lambda+c_{4}\,, $$

where,

$$ a_{3,4}=-\frac{\epsilon\pm\xi}{3}\,,~~~b_{3,4}=\frac{\epsilon}{9}(-11\epsilon\mp 2\xi)\,,~~~c_{3,4}=\pm\frac{2}{9}\epsilon\xi(\epsilon\pm\xi)\,. $$

Recall that for non-trivial fixed points to be real we need $\xi$ to be real as well as $\epsilon>\xi$ . Now examining the coefficients of the characteristic polynomials we see that the fixed point (41) has one negative eigenvalue and two positive eigenvalues, while (42) has two negative eigenvalues and one positive eigenvalue.

### A.3 Next order beta functions

In this subsection we list all diagrams in figure 13 contributing at the next order to the beta functions and renormalization of the fermionic self-energy. Notice that we list only diagrams which represent distinct graphs, whereas some diagrams in this list can include different sub-cases, like in figure 7.

*Figure 13: The next order diagrams contributing to renormalization of the couplings and self-energy.*

All the diagrams can be computed with the use of the integrals in eq. (58). The result of the computation is

$$ \displaystyle\beta_{U}^{(2)}= \displaystyle-\frac{\big((MM^{\prime}+1)U^{3}+(MM^{\prime}+5)UV^{2}+(M-M^{\prime})(2U^{2}V-V^{3})\big)(\pi-4\log(2))}{\pi^{2}A_{0}^{4}} \displaystyle-\frac{(M^{2}-1)\gamma^{2}U(\gamma_{E}-\log(4\pi))}{4\pi^{2}A_{0}^{2}M}\,, \displaystyle\beta_{V}^{(2)}= \displaystyle-\frac{V\big((MM^{\prime}+5)U^{2}+2MM^{\prime}V^{2}+2(M-M^{\prime})UV\big)(\pi-4\log(2))}{\pi^{2}A_{0}^{4}}-\frac{(M^{2}-1)\gamma^{2}V(\gamma_{E}-\log(4\pi))}{4\pi^{2}A_{0}^{2}M}\,, \displaystyle\beta_{\gamma}^{(2)}= \displaystyle-\frac{\big((MM^{\prime}-1)(U^{2}+V^{2})+2(M-M^{\prime})UV\big)\gamma(\pi-4\log(2))}{2\pi^{2}A_{0}^{4}}+\frac{\gamma^{3}(\gamma_{E}-\log(4\pi))}{8\pi^{2}A_{0}^{2}M}\,, $$

and $\beta_{\zeta}^{(2)}=0$ and $\delta_{c}^{(2)}=0$ , where $\gamma_{E}$ is the Euler constant. We see that there is no renormalization of the fermionic self-energy to this order and we can guess that this is true to all orders of the perturbation theory. We also notice that upon taking $\gamma=0$ , $M=2$ , $M^{\prime}=1$ and defining $\beta_{U}=(\beta_{U}+\beta_{V})|_{U+V\to U}$ we recover the result reported in [12].

## Appendix B Onset of spin glass order in a metal

This Appendix will address the transition from the disordered Fermi liquid phase to the metallic spin glass. There are 3 possible theories of this transition: (i) At large $U$ , and for $p>0$ , eliminate the doubly-occupied site, and address the transition in the $t$ - $J$ model. This yields a deconfined critical point, described in Ref. 10. (ii) At small $U$ , and at $p=0$ , perform the RG analysis presented in Section IV. This yields fixed point $FP_{3}$ , which could describe the onset of spin glass order in a metal. (iii) Use a weak-coupling Landau functional approach to quantum spin glasses [29, 13], which we review in this section.

We begin with the disordered-averaged imaginary time path integral of the Hamiltonian in (1), keeping track of replica indices, $a,b=1\ldots n$ ; at the end we need to take the $n\rightarrow 0$ limit. The path integral has the form

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{Z} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int\mathcal{D}Q^{ab}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\exp\left(-N\mathcal{S}[Q]\right) \displaystyle\mathcal{S}[Q] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{3J^{2}}{4}\int d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\sum_{ab}\left[Q^{ab}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\right]^{2}+\mathcal{S}_{1}[Q] $$

where the functional $\mathcal{S}_{1}[Q]$ is to obtained by a path integral over the electrons. Near the transition, it turns out to be sufficient to evaluate $\mathcal{S}_{1}[Q]$ in powers of $J^{2}$ and $U$ to understand the basic structure of the critical point, as in other theories of the onset of broken symmetry in metals [30]. Explicitly the expression is

$$ \displaystyle\exp\left(-N\mathcal{S}_{1}[Q]\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int\mathcal{D}R^{ab}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\exp\left(-\frac{Nt^{2}}{2}\left|R^{ab}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\right|^{2}-N\mathcal{S}_{2}[Q,R]\right) \displaystyle\exp\left(-\mathcal{S}_{2}[Q,R]\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int\mathcal{D}c_{\alpha}^{a}(\tau)\exp\left\{-\int d\tau\left[c_{\alpha}^{a\dagger}(\tau)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}-\mu\right)c_{\alpha}^{a}(\tau)+\frac{U}{2}c^{a\dagger}_{\alpha}(\tau)c^{a\dagger}_{\beta}(\tau)c_{\beta}^{a}(\tau)c_{\alpha}^{a}(\tau)\right]\right. \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\left.t^{2}\int d\tau d\tau^{\prime}R^{ab}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})c_{\alpha}^{a\dagger}(\tau)c_{\alpha}^{b}(\tau^{\prime})+\frac{J^{2}}{2}\int d\tau d\tau^{\prime}Q^{ab}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\bm{S}^{a}(\tau)\cdot\bm{S}^{b}(\tau^{\prime})\right\}, $$

where the second expression generalizes (4). Analyzing the saddle-point equations of (74) and (75) in the large $N$ limit, it can be verified that we obtain the replica generalizations of the self-consistency conditions in (5) and (6).

First, we explicitly solve the saddle-point equations for $R$ at $J^{2}=U=0$ . The solution is replica diagonal and depends only on time differences

$$ R^{ab}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})=\delta^{ab}R(\tau-\tau^{\prime})\,. $$

The equation for $R(\tau)$ is easily expressed in frequency space

$$ R(i\omega)=\frac{1}{i\omega+\mu-t^{2}R(i\omega)}\,, $$

and yields the Green’s function of a disordered Fermi liquid with the expected semi-circular density of the states

$$ R(i\omega)=\frac{1}{2t^{2}}\left(i\omega+\mu-\sqrt{(i\omega+\mu)^{2}-4t^{2}}\right)\,. $$

For $|\mu|<2t$ , we have a non-zero density of states at the Fermi level, and the low frequency behavior

$$ R(i\omega)=\frac{\mu}{2t^{2}}-\mbox{sgn}(\omega)\frac{\sqrt{4t^{2}-\mu^{2}}}{2t^{2}}\,. $$

This is just the Fourier transform of the electron Green’s function in (25) with $\Delta_{f}+\Delta_{b}=1/2$ .

Next we expand (75) in powers of $J^{2}$ and $U$ , and evaluate the path integral over the $c_{\alpha}^{a}$ . This results in an expression for $\mathcal{S}[Q]$ as a polynomial in the $Q^{ab}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ which has the form described in Ref. 13; see also Chapter 22 in Ref. 31. A crucial term in this expansion is a term linear in $Q$ of the form

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{J^{2}}{2}\int d\tau d\tau^{\prime}Q^{ab}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\left\langle\bm{S}^{a}(\tau)\cdot\bm{S}^{b}(\tau^{\prime})\right\rangle \displaystyle\sim \displaystyle-\frac{J^{2}}{2}\int d\tau d\tau^{\prime}\frac{Q^{aa}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})}{(\tau-\tau^{\prime})^{2}} \displaystyle\sim \displaystyle TJ^{2}\sum_{\omega_{n}}Q^{aa}(i\omega_{n},-i\omega_{n})\left[r+|\omega_{n}|\right]\,, $$

where $\omega_{n}=2\pi nT$ is a Matsubara frequency. The $1/\tau^{2}$ term is characteristic of the decay of spin correlations in a disordered Fermi liquid, a direct consequence of the constant density of states at the Fermi level in (79). The frequency dependence in (80) is primarily responsible for the low frequency dynamics of the spin glass order parameter, and the frequency depends of all the other terms in the action for $Q$ can be safely neglected. Near the critical point, it turns out to be sufficient to keep only the following terms in the effective action [13]

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{S}[Q] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{r}{\kappa}\int d\tau\,Q^{aa}(\tau,\tau)-\frac{1}{\pi\kappa}\int d\tau d\tau^{\prime}\,\frac{Q^{aa}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})}{(\tau-\tau^{\prime})^{2}} \displaystyle{-}\,\frac{\kappa}{3}\int d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}d\tau_{3}\sum_{abc}Q^{ab}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})Q^{bc}(\tau_{2},\tau_{3})Q^{ca}(\tau_{3},\tau_{1}){+}\,\frac{u}{2}\int d\tau\left[Q^{aa}(\tau,\tau)\right]^{2}\,. $$

Here we have performed a shift by an unimportant short-time correlator, $Q^{ab}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\rightarrow Q^{ab}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})-C\delta^{ab}\delta(\tau-\tau^{\prime})$ , to eliminate quadratic terms in the action similar to that in (74).

It is now a straightforward matter to solve the saddle point equations of (81). The saddle-point value $Q$ has the following structure in Matsubara frequency space

$$ Q^{ab}(i\omega_{n},i\epsilon_{n})=\frac{\delta_{\omega_{n},0}\delta_{\epsilon_{n},0}}{T^{2}}\,q^{ab}+\frac{\delta_{\omega_{n}+\epsilon_{n},0}}{T}\,\delta^{ab}\,Q(i\omega_{n})\,. $$

Here $q^{ab}$ is the spin-glass order parameter, which is non-zero only for the parameter $r$ (appearing in (80)) smaller than a critical value, $r<r_{c}$ . Focusing first on the Fermi liquid state found for $r>r_{c}$ , it was shown that the second term in (82) has the form

$$ Q(i\omega_{n})\sim-\sqrt{r-r_{c}+|\omega_{n}|}\quad,\quad r\geq r_{c}\,. $$

This quantity is just the Fourier transform of $Q(\tau)$ appearing in (5) and (6), and so at the critical point $r=r_{c}$ , the spin correlations decay as

$$ Q(\tau)\sim\frac{1}{|\tau|^{3/2}}\quad,\quad r=r_{c}\,. $$

Comparing with (35), we see that $\epsilon^{\prime}=-1/2$ . So the present critical point appears distinct from the fixed point $FP_{3}$ found in Section IV, which can satisfy the self-consistency conditions only for $\epsilon^{\prime}>0$ .

Finally, let us also recall [29, 13] the nature of the solution for $r<r_{c}$ . Here the spin glass order parameter $q^{ab}$ is non-zero. In the simplest replica-symmetric ansatz, $q^{ab}=q_{EA}$ , the Edwards-Anderson order parameter for all $a$ and $b$ , and

$$ q_{EA}\sim r_{c}-r\quad,\quad r<r_{c} $$

At $T>0$ , the stable solution has replica symmetry breaking, but the structure of this is very similar to that of the classical spin glass. The replica diagonal term $Q(\tau)$ in (82) is the only one with non-trivial time dependence, and this remains pinned at the $r=r_{c}$ form in (84) for $r<r_{c}$ .
